issues.description: The abstract and multiple sections describe the sample as a 'national probability sample' and 'nationally representative sample,' yet the Methods section states participants were 'recruited through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.' A university student convenience sample is fundamentally different from a national probability sample. The average age of 19 years, 68% female composition, and 86% Pākehā identification further confirm this is a student sample, not a nationally representative one. This mischaracterization severely undermines the generalizability claims made throughout the paper and contradicts the authors' own argument that general population samples yield different results than student samples.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington... the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The entire rationale for the study rests on the argument that Stanley et al. (2014) found RWA (not SDO) to be the stronger predictor because they used a student sample, and that a general population sample would show SDO as the stronger predictor. However, the present study also uses a student sample (introductory psychology pool), completely undermining the stated rationale and the interpretation of results. The authors interpret their findings as consistent with general population patterns, when their sample is the same type (students) that they argued produces different results.
issues.quote: The present paper advances this research by examining the impact of SDO and RWA on environment-related attitudes in a general population sample, spanning five years.

issues.description: The Strengths and Limitations section explicitly claims the research uses a 'nationally representative sample' with 'highly generalisable' results. This is false given the student convenience sample described in the Methods. This misrepresentation affects the entire framing of the paper's contribution.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing the predictive strength of SDO vs. RWA on environmentalism was non-significant (χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126), yet the authors conclude that 'SDO is a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA.' This interpretation contradicts the statistical test they performed specifically to evaluate this claim. The authors cannot claim SDO is a significantly stronger predictor when their own formal test fails to reject the null hypothesis of equal predictive strength.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data χ2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The reported chi-square difference test for comparing the SDO→RWA and RWA→SDO paths yields an extraordinarily large value (χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001) for a single degree of freedom test. This value is implausible for a sample of 374 participants and likely reflects a computational error, model misspecification, or reporting error. This needs verification and explanation.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (χ2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: The CFI of .86 is below the conventional threshold of .90 (and well below the more stringent .95 threshold). The authors dismiss this poor fit by attributing it to 'model complexity,' but poor CFI can also indicate model misspecification. Selectively accepting fit indices that support the model while dismissing those that do not is problematic. The very large chi-square (36511.73) also suggests substantial misfit. The rationale for accepting the model despite poor fit is insufficient.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The authors used listwise deletion for a five-wave longitudinal study. Attrition over five years in a student sample is likely substantial, and listwise deletion can introduce severe bias if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR). Modern approaches such as full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation are standard for handling missing data in longitudinal SEM/path analysis and would be more appropriate. The authors do not report attrition rates or patterns of missingness.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: For a five-year longitudinal study, no information is provided about attrition rates, patterns of dropout, or comparisons between completers and non-completers. The authors refer readers to the NZAVS website for details, but this critical information should be reported in the manuscript to evaluate potential attrition bias.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The environmentalism measure assesses concern about environmental problems ('How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'), yet the variable is labeled and discussed as 'willingness to sacrifice for the environment' and 'willingness to change behaviour.' These are conceptually distinct constructs—environmental concern vs. behavioral willingness. The mismatch between what was measured and what is claimed to have been measured affects the validity of the conclusions.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale... willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL)

issues.subcategory: Path analysis instead of latent variable modeling
issues.description: The authors use path analysis with observed (manifest) variables rather than structural equation modeling with latent variables. With only 2 items for environmentalism and abbreviated scales for SDO and RWA, measurement error is not accounted for, which can bias cross-lagged estimates. Given the acknowledged low reliabilities, latent variable modeling would have been more appropriate to separate true score variance from measurement error.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: Despite acknowledging the limitations of cross-sectional data for causal inference, the authors make causal claims based on their cross-lagged panel model. Cross-lagged panel models do not establish causation, and recent methodological literature (e.g., Hamaker et al., 2015) has shown that traditional CLPM conflates between-person and within-person effects, potentially producing misleading results. The authors use language like 'causal pathway,' 'causal effect,' and 'influence' throughout.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism. The motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance

issues.subcategory: Cross-lagged panel model limitations not acknowledged
issues.description: The traditional cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) used here has been criticized for conflating between-person and within-person variance (Hamaker, Kuiper, & Grasman, 2015). A random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) would be more appropriate for separating trait-like stability from within-person change processes. The authors do not acknowledge this limitation or consider alternative modeling approaches.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: Environmentalism is measured with only two items, which severely limits the reliability and content validity of this construct. A two-item measure cannot adequately capture the breadth of environmental attitudes, and the reliability of such a short scale is inherently limited. No reliability estimate is reported for this measure.
issues.quote: "How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?" and "To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?"

issues.description: The Methods section states a significance threshold of p < .05, but Figure 1's caption states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are contradictory thresholds, creating confusion about which criterion was actually applied.
issues.quote: we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings... All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: The authors state they adopted p < .05 'because of the large sample size,' but typically a large sample size would motivate a more stringent threshold (not the conventional one), as large samples can detect trivially small effects. The justification is backwards.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: Both SDO and RWA were measured with only 6 items each (from longer scales), and the authors acknowledge that reliabilities were 'poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used.' The reported alphas of .69 and .70 are below the conventional .70 threshold (or barely at it), which combined with path analysis (no latent variables) means measurement error could substantially attenuate or bias the cross-lagged estimates.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures

issues.subcategory: Missing RWA item at one time point
issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2, meaning the RWA measure differs across time points (5 items at T2 vs. 6 items at other time points). This creates a measurement inconsistency that could affect the stationarity assumption and comparability of scores across time. The authors do not discuss how this was handled or its potential impact.
issues.quote: The item "Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The model has 2279 degrees of freedom, which seems very high for a path analysis with 3 observed variables across 5 time points. A standard cross-lagged path model with 15 observed variables would have far fewer degrees of freedom. This suggests the model may be at the item level rather than the composite level, but this is not clearly described. The discrepancy needs explanation.

The Methods section describes the model as 'path analysis' examining associations between three variables across five time points, but the degrees of freedom (2279) and the mention of constraining 'residual variance for the same item over time' suggest the model operates at the item level. The actual model specification is unclear and insufficiently described.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment... we constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: The same sentence about constraining cross-lagged associations appears twice in the Data Analysis section, suggesting a copy-editing error.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The authors state they 'present standardized parameters' but Figure 1 caption says 'Unstandardized parameters.' The text reports unstandardized coefficients (B values). This inconsistency is confusing.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances... Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment

issues.description: The cross-lagged effects are very small (B = -.11 for SDO→WILL, B = -.02 for RWA→WILL), yet the authors interpret these as substantively meaningful without discussing effect sizes or practical significance. Given the small magnitude of effects, the practical implications discussed at length in the Discussion may be overstated.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The authors report 'SD' alongside the unstandardized coefficients (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'), but in the context of parameter estimates, this should be the standard error (SE), not the standard deviation. This is either a reporting error or a misuse of terminology.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001)

issues.subcategory: Confound of sample type with study design
issues.description: The authors attribute differences between their findings and Stanley et al. (2014) to sample type (students vs. general population), but the studies also differ in duration (5 months vs. 5 years), number of time points (2 vs. 5), and measures used. The attribution to sample type alone is not justified when multiple factors differ between studies.
issues.quote: However, this difference in findings is consistent with expectations based on the results of Stanley and Wilson's [22] meta-analysis, which showed that the association with SDO is significantly weaker in student samples.

issues.description: Table 1 reports the correlation between RWA and WILL as -.08 with CI [-.11, -.05], yet the text states 'the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.' The CI for SDO-WILL is [-.27, -.22] and for RWA-WILL is [-.11, -.05]. While these don't overlap, this method of comparing correlations by CI overlap is conservative and not the recommended approach for testing whether two correlations differ significantly.
issues.quote: the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.

issues.description: Figure 1 is referenced but not included in the manuscript. The reader cannot evaluate the autoregressive paths, cross-lagged paths, or overall model structure without seeing the figure.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time

issues.description: Multiple spelling errors throughout the manuscript: 'stonger' (stronger), 'sarcity' (scarcity), 'situatoinal' (situational), 'nonexistant' (nonexistent), 'analagous' (analogous), 'New Zealander's' (New Zealanders). While minor individually, collectively they suggest insufficient proofreading.
issues.quote: SDO has a stonger influence... resource sarcity... These situatoinal factors... weak or nonexistant... This finding is analagous... New Zealander's are socialized

issues.description: Multiple cross-lagged paths and chi-square difference tests are conducted without any correction for multiple comparisons. Given the number of tests performed, some findings (particularly those with p-values near .05) may be inflated.

The study spans five semesters from 2009 to 2013, but it is unclear whether the time intervals between measurement occasions are equal. If participants were assessed each semester (twice per year), the intervals may vary. Unequal intervals can affect the interpretation of cross-lagged effects in a stationarity-constrained model, but this is not discussed.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: The authors impose a stationarity constraint (time-invariant parameters) without testing whether this assumption holds. Given that the study spans ages ~19-24 (a period of significant developmental change), the assumption that cross-lagged effects are constant over time may not be warranted. The authors justify this by saying they are 'more interested in the overall and comparative effects,' but this does not validate the assumption.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.description: Reference 26 (Sibley C. New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study) is incomplete—it lacks year, volume, pages, or URL. It appears to be a reference to a website or technical document but is insufficiently cited.
issues.quote: Sibley C. New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study.

issues.description: Participants were recruited from an introductory psychology course and participated across five semesters. Students in psychology courses may be subject to demand characteristics or social desirability effects, particularly regarding environmental attitudes. Additionally, repeated participation over semesters may lead to testing effects. These potential threats to validity are not discussed.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington.

issues.subcategory: Reliability not reported for environmentalism measure
issues.description: While reliabilities are reported for SDO (.69) and RWA (.70) in Table 1, the reliability for the two-item environmentalism measure (.76) is reported in the table but not discussed in the text. More importantly, with only two items, Cronbach's alpha is equivalent to the Spearman-Brown corrected correlation, and the adequacy of this measure deserves more discussion.
issues.quote: WILL ... .76

issues.subcategory: Confidence interval for RWA cross-lagged path
issues.description: The 95% CI for the RWA→environmentalism path is reported as [-.05, -.01], which is quite wide relative to the point estimate of -.02, suggesting considerable uncertainty about the magnitude of this effect. This uncertainty is not adequately discussed.
